pedagogy.summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark — on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below — plus the frame-dependent left and right. Children perceive these relations early and describe them with vague words ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and to model them in everyday talk. Positions are relative and abstract (whether something is 'behind' depends on the landmark and the viewer's side), so the deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right, which depend on the direction the child faces and are not mastered until early elementary school.
bestPractices: Model correct language in reply to vague answers: when a child says 'over there' and points, recast it — 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet'.
Name the landmark explicitly as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa') so position is heard as a relation, not a property of the object.
Embed the words in daily routines and directional games — table-setting ('cups next to the plates, juice in the middle'), hopscotch, board games with forward/back.
Build left and right on the body first (a sticker on the right hand, shaking hands) before applying them to objects; be patient and don't treat early errors as failure.
Have the child both FOLLOW and GIVE instructions ('put the cube behind the box') so the vocabulary becomes a productive tool, not just receptive.
keyRepresentations: Object–landmark–relation triples acted out with real toys and objects
The child's own body, with a right-hand sticker, for left and right
Everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — and simple picture scenes to describe
Barrier games: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for a partner to reproduce it
commonMisconceptions: Uses vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one') with a gesture instead of a positional word
Judges left/right from the child's own current facing and cannot adjust it for an object or person facing the other way
Cannot hold two relations at once — a thing that is above one object and below another is described with only one relation (egocentrism / dual relations)
Treats a position as belonging to the object ('the front') rather than as a relation to a named landmark and a viewpoint

learn.summary: Positional language names WHERE things are relative to a landmark (on, under, behind, in front of, next to, above, below, left, right). Left/right, and behind/in front of when the landmark has no front of its own (e.g. a plain box), depend on viewpoint. Young children (4-6) perceive these relations early but describe them vaguely ('over there', with a point); the teaching job is to attach precise words to the concepts and model them in everyday talk as object + landmark + relation ('the ball is behind the sofa'). The deepest difficulties are holding two relations at once (dual relations) and left/right. Left/right for objects and for people facing you depends on viewpoint and is typically not mastered until early elementary school. Because this is a language-in-context topic, the core goal is productive AND receptive use: the child should both FOLLOW and GIVE positional instructions, not merely recognise words.

activities.title: Place the object: follow spoken positional instructions
feedback: When the relation is correct, confirm concretely: 'yes — the teddy is behind the box.'

When the object is placed in the wrong relation (e.g. beside instead of behind), show where the correct relation is from the child's own viewpoint (for a plain box, 'behind' is the side away from the child) — for example gently outline or point to the 'behind' location, then let the child try again.
Optional interactive version: a correct drop settles with a happy chime; a wrong drop highlights/outlines the target relation so 'behind' is shown, not just told.
activities.rationale: Children locate things early but must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; pairing each word with a named landmark (object–landmark–relation) and acting it out is intended to make position heard as a relation rather than a property of the object.
sourceClaims: Young children locate things but use vague, informal language and must learn both the positional words and the concepts they refer to; adults should model correct language and use landmarks (object–landmark–relation). Left and right are notoriously difficult and frame-dependent (relative to the direction the child faces), typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early failure should not be over-corrected. Holding dual relations at once (a thing above one object and below another) is hard because young children are egocentric. Everyday routines and directional games (table-setting, hopscotch, board games) build the vocabulary.
learnerActions: Listen to a spoken instruction naming an object, a landmark, and a relation, e.g. 'put the teddy behind the box'.
Move the named object into the correct relation to the landmark (for example drag it in a bedroom scene, or place a real toy with a real box and cup).
Try a short series that varies the relation: 'put the cup next to the teddy', 'put the pencil under the book'.
activities.intendedInsight: A positional word is an instruction that tells you exactly where to put something relative to a named landmark.

activities.title: Your turn to tell me: give the instruction (barrier / role-flip)
feedback: When the child names a relation and landmark the partner can act on, celebrate that the word worked: 'you said behind the box, so I put it right there.'
If the child falls back on 'there' with a gesture, recast into a usable instruction ('do you mean next to the cup?') and invite them to try the word themselves.

Optional interactive version: the child taps a relation word ('behind' / 'in front of' / 'next to'), a cartoon friend places its object to match, and the two scenes snap together when the word was right.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is both words and concepts, asking the child to produce (not just recognise) an instruction is intended to turn the vocabulary into a usable tool and to show whether the child has both the words and the concepts: a precise relation plus landmark is hard to produce by chance, so giving instructions is proposed as a way to distinguish genuine use from receptive familiarity. This production-discrimination logic is an unvalidated design proposal, not a source-established finding.

learnerActions: Place or choose where a toy goes, then TELL a partner (adult, another child, or a cartoon friend) where it is using a precise positional word and a named landmark, e.g. 'behind the box'.
Have the partner act only on what the child says, so the child sees whether the word carried the meaning.
Play a barrier game: the child describes a hidden layout precisely enough for the partner to reproduce it without seeing it.
activities.intendedInsight: A position word is a tool that carries meaning to someone else — when I say the right relation and landmark, my partner can act correctly without seeing or pointing.

activities.title: In-role conversation: answering 'where is it?'
feedback: Recast vague deictic answers into the precise form instead of marking them wrong: 'yes — next to the cup.'
Affirm when the child supplies a relation and landmark unprompted.
activities.rationale: As a language-use topic, an in-role dialogue is intended to elicit productive spoken use and to model precise words in context (the source supports adults modelling correct language); its narrow observable limit is that it does not provide the concrete manipulate-and-see feedback of a placing game, so it complements rather than replaces that activity. Its comparative efficacy is untested.

learnerActions: Respond in role when a character asks 'where's the teddy?', answering with a positional word and landmark rather than a point.
Let the character act on the answer so the child hears whether it was clear.
Have the character gently model precise words by recasting vague answers ('over there' → 'yes, on the shelf next to the coat closet').
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday talk is where positional words become natural: naming the relation and landmark lets someone find or place a thing without seeing where you point.

activities.title: Build left and right on the body first
feedback: Reinforce correct own-body left/right with the sticker anchor.
When the child reverses left/right for a facing partner or a turned object, do not drill it as failure — acknowledge it is tricky, keep exposure, and expect later maturation.
activities.rationale: Left and right are frame-dependent and notoriously difficult, typically not mastered until early elementary school, so early errors should not be over-corrected (as the source notes). Building them on the body first with a right-hand sticker is a recommended scaffold for anchoring the terms before applying them to objects; this specific method comes from the row's best-practice synthesis rather than being prescribed by the source.

learnerActions: Put a sticker on the right hand and use it as an anchor for 'left' and 'right'.
Play own-body directional games — shaking hands with the right hand, raising the left foot.
Later, try applying left/right to objects, with the adult expecting errors and not over-correcting.
activities.intendedInsight: Left and right start from my own body; applying them to objects and to people facing me is harder and comes later.

activities.title: Embed positional words in daily routines and games
feedback: Keep supplying positional language in routines and recast vague answers; expect precise words to firm up gradually rather than immediately.
Notice and name when the child uses a relation + landmark during a real routine.

When a target sits between two landmarks, accept the one relation the child gives and add the second in a recast ('yes, on top of the red block — and it's also under the shelf') rather than forcing both at once.
activities.rationale: Everyday routines and directional games build the vocabulary in meaningful context and give repeated authentic practice across varied scenes, as the source notes.

Describe everyday scenes — a set table, a shelf, a bedroom — naming object, landmark, and relation.
activities.intendedInsight: Positional words belong in everyday talk, not just lessons; using them in routines firms up the vocabulary over time.

constraints: The core objective is productive AND receptive USE: the child must both follow and give instructions. Recognition-only tasks (matching or categorising position words to pictures) can check recognition but do not by themselves elicit independent production, so they cannot alone demonstrate mastery of this language-in-context topic — use them, if at all, only as a recognition check.

Tapping a static picture scene to reveal position words is useful for exposure, but on its own it does not let the child produce instructions or receive manipulate-and-see feedback; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective. This is a scope limit, not a claim that static images cannot teach.

Do not mark vague deictic language ('over there', 'this one' with a point) as an error for 4-6 year olds: informal language normally precedes precise words. Recast and keep supplying positional language, expecting it to firm up over time.

Do not drill left/right for facing partners/turned objects as failure, and do not force two relations (above AND below) at once: both are developmentally hard and typically not mastered until early elementary school. Accept one relation and add the second in a recast.

A rotatable 3D scene could make frame-dependence (how behind/in front and left/right flip as you move around) felt, but that perspective-taking is the hard part not expected at 4-6 and exceeds the core naming goal; it is an optional enrichment, not required.

Always pair a position word with a named landmark. Move the object to new places to show that position is a relation to the landmark, not a fixed feature of the object. As light, optional enrichment, moving the viewer around a landmark with no front of its own (e.g. a plain box) can show that 'behind' depends on where you stand. For landmarks with their own front (a sofa, a person), 'behind' usually means the landmark's own back.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The single cited source (DREME Network / Stanford) supports the general principles (model language, use object–landmark–relation, left/right and dual relations are developmentally late, use routines/games). It does not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format (placing game vs. dialogue vs. 3D scene); legacy catalog claims such as 'a static image cannot teach' or '3D exceeds the goal' have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

The production-discriminates-mastery logic (activity 2) and the efficacy of the dialogue format (activity 3) come from the original row's own assessment analysis and remain untested proposals; efficacy wording has been qualified accordingly.
The body-first-with-sticker scaffold for left/right (activity 4) is from the row's best-practice synthesis; the source supports only the late-mastery and patience principle, not this specific method.
Receptive-only formats are limited only in the narrow, observable sense that recognition does not itself elicit production — this is not a claim about which medium is superior.

probeDeeper: You told me the teddy is 'there' — if I close my eyes, can you tell me a word so I know exactly where it is without pointing?
You said it's on your left. If I come and sit on the other side of the table, is it still on my left?
The pencil is on top of the book. Is anything above the pencil too?
Put the cube 'behind' the box — now if you turn the box around, is the cube still behind it?
assess.correctAnswer: Follows each positional instruction by placing the object in the correct relation, and, when giving the instruction, uses a precise positional word (behind / next to / on top of / under) together with a named landmark, so the teacher can act on it unambiguously — not a vague 'there' with a point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Says 'over there' or 'this one' with a point instead of a position word ('put it... there!')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT mark this as an error — vague informal language normally precedes precise words; recast it ('yes, next to the cup') and keep supplying positional language in routines, expecting it to firm up over time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When GIVING an instruction, gestures or says 'there' rather than naming a relation

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses left/right fixed to their own body, so it is wrong for an object or a person facing the other way ('it's on the left' — but only from where I'm sitting)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill this as a failure — left/right is frame-dependent and typically not mastered until early elementary school; reinforce own-body left/right (sticker) and keep exposure, expecting later maturation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives or follows left/right correctly for self but reverses it for a facing partner or a turned object

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot say a thing is above one object and below another at the same time ('it's on top' — ignoring what is above it)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT push both relations at once — accept the one they give and add the second in your recast ('yes, on top of the red block — and it's also under the shelf'), letting the coordination develop.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When a target sits between two landmarks, describes only one relation

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a position word as a fixed feature of the object rather than a relation to a landmark ('the front', with no reference to what it is in front of)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always pair the word with a named landmark and physically move the viewer or the object to show that 'behind' changes with viewpoint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names a position with no landmark, or insists 'behind' is a fixed side of the object regardless of the viewer

responseLevels.gap: Relies on gesture and 'there / this one'; follows only the most familiar single instruction; cannot produce a usable positional instruction.
responseLevels.full: Uses precise positional words productively and receptively across new scenes, names the landmark, and begins to coordinate two relations and adjust for viewpoint (relational) — with a full grasp of left/right for others expected only later.
responseLevels.partial: Follows and produces common single relations (on / under / behind / next to) with a named landmark in simple familiar setups, but breaks down on left/right for a facing partner, on dual relations, or in an unfamiliar scene — handling one relation at a time without coordinating them (multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set up a real or pictured scene with a box, a toy and a cup. Give a short series of doing-instructions and one telling task, and watch/listen for USE: 'Put the teddy behind the box. ... Now put the cup next to the teddy. ... Now YOU tell me where to put the pencil, so I can do exactly what you say.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has both the words and the concepts follows correctly AND produces a usable instruction that names a relation and a landmark. A child with only receptive familiarity may follow simple cases but, when asked to give an instruction, falls back on 'there' with a gesture or names the object with no relation — revealing the word is not yet a tool. Requiring production is the discriminator: a precise relation cannot be produced by luck.
